p.src: Sanshirō’s spirit began to drift. When he listened to a lecture, it seemed to come from far away. At worst, he would fail to write down something essential. At its worst, he felt as though he were renting someone else’s ears for a fee. Sanshirō found the whole thing unbearably absurd. At a loss for what else to do, he told Yojirō that lately the lectures had somehow ceased to interest him. Yojirō’s answer was always the same. “Of course lectures aren’t interesting. You’re a country boy, so you imagined they would eventually amount to something grand, and that’s why you’ve patiently listened to them until now, isn’t it? The height of folly. Their lectures have been like this since the dawn of creation. There’s no point being disappointed now.” “That isn’t quite it…” Sanshirō protested. The mismatch between Yojirō’s glib, flippant tone and Sanshirō’s ponderous way of speaking was extremely comical. After they had repeated this exchange two or three times, nearly half a month had passed before he knew it. Little by little, Sanshirō’s ears began to feel like his own again. Then it was Yojirō’s turn to say to Sanshirō, “You have a peculiar look on your face. You look exactly as though you were weary of life. It’s a fin-de-siècle face,” he pronounced. To this judgment as well, Sanshirō merely continued to repeat, “That isn’t quite it…” Sanshirō had not yet breathed enough artificial air to be delighted by a phrase like “fin de siècle.” Nor was he sufficiently acquainted with the ways of a certain society to use the phrase as an amusing plaything. Only the phrase “weary of life” appealed to him a little. Indeed, he did seem to be growing tired. Sanshirō did not think it was due solely to his diarrhea. Yet his outlook on life was not fashionable enough for him to parade a profoundly weary face. And so the conversation went no further.

He made quite a few circuits of the university pond, but nothing in particular happened. He also walked back and forth in front of the hospital any number of times, but met only ordinary people. If he went to Ōkubo next time and talked at leisure, he would most likely learn both her name and her background, so he left without pressing the matter. p.src: The more Sanshirō drifted along, the more cheerful he became. At first he had concentrated so intensely on the lectures that his ears seemed to fail him and he had trouble taking notes, but lately he listened only as closely as seemed reasonable, so it no longer bothered him. During lectures he thought about all sorts of things. He did not even mind missing a little of what was said. On looking closely, he found that Yojirō and everyone else did the same. Sanshirō began to think that this was probably as much as one needed to do. Amid Sanshirō's many thoughts, that familiar ribbon would appear from time to time. Whenever it did, he grew uneasy. He became exceedingly unhappy. He would feel like setting off for Ōkubo at once. But after a while, some chain of associations or stimulus from the outside world would distract him. Thus, on the whole, he remained carefree. And so he went on dreaming. He showed no sign of actually going to Ōkubo. One afternoon, Sanshirō was strolling as usual when, from the top of Dangozaka, he turned left and came out onto the broad avenue of Sendagi Hayashichō. It was fine autumn weather, and lately even the Tokyo sky looked as deep as the sky in the countryside. The mere thought of living beneath such a sky cleared his head. And if he could get out into the open country, there would be nothing more to wish for. His spirits expanded freely, and his soul grew as vast as the open sky. Yet at the same time, his whole body grew taut and firm. It was unlike the loose, languid mildness of spring. Gazing at the hedges on either side, Sanshirō walked on, breathing in his first autumn in Tokyo. At the foot of the slope, the chrysanthemum-figure exhibition had opened only two or three days before. When he rounded the bend in the slope, he had even seen its banners. Now only the sound could be heard, the distant thump and clang of the festival music. The sound of the music gradually floated up from below and spread throughout the crystal-clear autumn air, until at last it became an exceedingly tenuous wave. Its lingering ripple reached the edge of Sanshirō's eardrums and naturally came to rest there.

p.src: From there he went out to Yanaka, circled around through Nezu, and returned to his lodgings in Hongō toward evening. Sanshirō felt that he had spent a more carefree half-day than he had known in quite some time. When he went to the university the next day, Yojirō was not there. From five to six there was a lecture shared by all students in the purely literary disciplines. Sanshirō attended it. It was too dark to take notes. Yet it was too early to turn on the electric lights. It was the hour when the depths beyond the branches of the great zelkova visible outside the long, narrow windows were gradually turning black, so that the lecturer's face and the students' faces were equally indistinct within the room. Consequently, it felt somehow mysterious, like eating a steamed bun in the dark. Sanshirō thought there was something curious about not understanding the lecture. We were supposed to move last month, but I put it off until the day after tomorrow, the Emperor's Birthday, so no matter what, I have to find a place by the end of tomorrow. Do you know of anywhere?” he asked. For all his urgency now, yesterday he had idled the day away in a manner that left it impossible to tell whether he was strolling or house-hunting. Sanshirō could make almost no sense of it. Yojirō explained that this was because the professor had been with him. “It was a mistake to have the professor looking for a house in the first place. He's a man who has never looked for one in his life, but something must have come over him yesterday. Thanks to him, I got a terrible scolding at the Satake residence and ended up looking like a perfect fool. —Come now, don't you know of anywhere?” he suddenly pressed. It seemed that this was Yojirō's sole purpose in coming. When Sanshirō questioned him closely about the cause, he learned that the present landlord was a usurer who raised the rent recklessly; infuriated by this, Yojirō himself had announced that they would move out. He was loose and disorderly at the best of times, and today the house-hunting had made him somewhat agitated besides. He was an exceedingly honest man, but so quick-tempered that he sometimes beat his wife with a piece of firewood. —Lying in bed, Sanshirō even recalled how Shinzō had first begun keeping bees. That had been about five years earlier.

When they went to see it, they found, or so the letter said, a monument of granite standing amid the red earth of a yard where neither tree nor grass grew. The letter said that Heitaro was proud of that granite. It had taken several days to quarry it from the mountain, and then the stonemason had charged him ten yen. Farmers and such might not understand these things, but since the young master of your house was studying at the university, he would surely know good stone from bad. So, he had apparently said, ask him about it the next time you write, and have him praise the monument I spent a whole ten yen making for my father. —Sanshirō began chuckling to himself. This was far more intense than the stone gate at Sendagi. The letter asked him to send a photograph of himself in his university uniform. p.src: Lying in bed, Sanshirō set these three worlds side by side and compared them with one another. Then he mixed the three worlds together and drew a single conclusion from them. —In short, nothing could be better than bringing his mother up from the country, taking a beautiful wife, and then devoting himself to scholarship. The conclusion was exceedingly commonplace. But since he had considered all manner of things before reaching it, it did not seem quite so commonplace to the thinker himself, who was apt to raise or lower the value of a conclusion according to the labor spent in thought. The only trouble was that this would make one insignificant wife stand for the vast third world. There were many beautiful women. A beautiful woman could be translated in many different ways. —Following Professor Hirota's example, Sanshirō tried using the word “translate.” —So long as they could be translated into the language of personality, he must come into contact with as many beautiful women as possible, broadening the sphere of influence produced by such translation and thereby bringing his own individuality to completion. p.src: Presently, the bell at the Higher School began to ring for the ceremony celebrating the Emperor's Birthday. Listening to the bell, Sanshirō supposed that it must be nine o'clock. Just as it finally occurred to him that he ought not to sit idle and might at least sweep up the dead cherry leaves, he remembered once more that there was no broom. He sat down on the veranda again. He had been sitting there perhaps two minutes when the garden gate quietly swung open. And, to his utter surprise, the woman from the pond appeared in the garden. Two sides were enclosed by hedges. The square garden measured less than ten tsubo. The instant Sanshirō saw the woman from the pond standing within this narrow enclosure, he understood at once. —Flowers must always be cut and admired within a vase. At that moment Sanshirō rose from the veranda. The woman stepped away from the folding gate. “Excuse me, but…” With these words by way of introduction, the woman bowed. As before, she inclined her body forward from the waist, but never lowered her face. Even as she bowed, she kept her eyes fixed on Sanshirō. Seen from the front, the woman's throat stretched long. At the same instant, her eyes were reflected in Sanshirō's pupils. Two or three days earlier, Sanshirō's aesthetics professor had shown him paintings by Greuze. On that occasion, the professor had explained that every portrait of a woman painted by this artist was rich in voluptuous expression. Voluptuous! There was no other word with which to describe the look in the pond woman's eyes at that moment. They were making some appeal. They appealed with something alluring. And their appeal was unmistakably directed at the senses. Yet it was an appeal that passed through the bones of sensuality and penetrated to the marrow. p.src: “Is this where Mr. Hirota is moving?” “Yes, this is the place.” Compared with the woman's voice and manner, Sanshirō's reply was exceedingly blunt. Sanshirō himself was aware of it. But he could think of no other way to put it. “Hasn't he moved in yet?” The woman's words were crisp and distinct. She did not let her endings trail off as people ordinarily did. “He hasn't come yet. He should be here soon.” The woman hesitated for a moment. She carried a large basket in her hand. As usual, Sanshirō could make nothing of the woman's kimono. He noticed only that, unlike usual, it did not gleam. The fabric had a strangely knobbly texture. And it bore something that might have been stripes or a pattern. The pattern was utterly haphazard. From time to time, cherry leaves drifted down from above. One of them landed on the lid of the basket. No sooner had it landed than the wind carried it away. The wind enveloped the woman. She stood in the midst of autumn. “And you are…?” By the time the wind had passed into the neighboring garden, the woman put the question to Sanshirō. “I've been asked to come and clean,” he said; but since she had caught him sitting there in a daze, Sanshirō found his own answer amusing. p.src: Sanshirō and Mineko looked at each other and laughed. Since the man in charge had stopped working, the two of them also held back from sorting any more books. Sanshirō pulled out a book of poetry. Mineko opened a large art album on her lap. Near the kitchen, the temporarily hired rickshaw man and the maid were arguing heatedly. They were making a tremendous racket. “Have a look at this,” Mineko said softly. Sanshirō leaned forward hesitantly and peered over the album. The scent of perfume came from Mineko’s hair. The picture depicted a mermaid. Below the naked woman’s waist was the body of a fish, which curved around her hips so that only the tail appeared on the far side. The woman faced outward, combing her long hair and catching the strands that passed through the comb in her other hand. A vast sea formed the background. “A mermaid.” “A mermaid.” Their heads almost touching, the two whispered the same words. Just then, for some reason, Yojirō rose from where he had been sitting cross-legged and came out into the corridor, saying, “What is it? What are you looking at?” The three put their heads together and turned through the album page by page. They offered all manner of comments. Every one of them was utterly casual. At that moment Professor Hirota returned in a frock coat from the ceremony for the Emperor’s Birthday. When the three greeted him, they turned the album face down. The professor suggested that they at least finish putting away the books, so the three set diligently to work again. With the master of the house now present, they apparently could no longer idle so freely, and an hour later, one way or another, all the books in the corridor had been crammed onto the shelves. The four stood side by side and surveyed the neatly arranged books. “We’ll finish organizing them tomorrow,” said Yojirō. His tone all but said, You’ll have to be satisfied with this. “You’ve collected quite a lot,” said Mineko. Finally Sanshirō asked, “Professor, have you read all these books?”

p.src: The maid brought tea from the kitchen. The company gathered around the basket began eating the sandwiches. For a little while they were quiet, but then, as though suddenly remembering something, Yojirō addressed Professor Hirota again. “Professor, while I have the chance, there’s something I’d like to ask. It’s about that Behn or whatever her name was.” “Aphra Behn?” “Who exactly was this Aphra Behn?” “An English woman of letters. From the seventeenth century.” “The seventeenth century is far too old. She would be no use as material for a magazine.” “She is old. But she is famous for being the first woman to make novel-writing her profession.” “It won’t do if she is famous. Let me ask a little more. What sort of things did she write?” “I have read only a novel called Oroonoko. Ogawa, there was a novel by that name in the collected works, wasn’t there?” Sanshirō had forgotten it completely. When he asked the professor for a synopsis, he was told that it concerned an African prince named Oroonoko who was deceived by an English captain, sold into slavery, and made to suffer terribly. Moreover, later generations had believed the story to be based on events the author herself had witnessed. “That is interesting. Miss Satomi, why don’t you try writing an Oroonoko yourself?” Yojirō turned to Mineko again. “I would not mind writing one, but I have never witnessed anything like that.” “If you need a dark-skinned hero, why not use our friend Ogawa here? He is from Kyushu and has a dark complexion.” “What a wicked tongue,” Mineko said as though defending Sanshirō; but immediately afterward she turned toward him and asked, “May I write it?” When Sanshirō saw her eyes, he remembered the woman as she had appeared that morning through the folding gate, carrying the basket. He felt intoxicated without having drunk.

p.src: Professor Hirota began smoking, as usual. Yojirō described this as blowing the smoke of philosophy through his nostrils. Indeed, the way the smoke emerged was rather unusual. Two thick, sturdy columns drifted serenely out through the openings. Yojirō gazed at those columns of smoke in silence, his back still half resting against the paper doors. Sanshirō’s eyes rested vaguely on the garden. It did not look like a house move. It looked altogether like a small social gathering. The conversation was correspondingly relaxed. Only Mineko, behind Professor Hirota, began folding the Western clothes he had discarded a little earlier. It appeared that Mineko was also responsible for getting the professor into Japanese dress. “About that Oronoko story just now—you’re careless, and I don’t want you getting it wrong, so I may as well mention something.” The professor’s smoke briefly ceased. “Yes, I’ll be sure to remember it,” Yojirō replied earnestly. “After that novel appeared, a man named Southerne made a separate stage play from the story. It has the same title, too. You mustn’t confuse the two.” “No, sir, I won’t confuse them.” Mineko, who had been folding the clothes, glanced at Yojirō’s face. “There is a famous line in that play. The line is ‘Pity’s akin to love’...” Having said only that, he once again vigorously blew out the smoke of philosophy. “It sounds as though Japan ought to have a saying like that too,” Sanshirō said this time. The others all agreed that there probably was. Yet none of them could recall one. They decided they might as well try translating it, and all four made various attempts, but nothing satisfactory emerged. At last Yojirō said, “This simply has to be done in the style of a popular song. The spirit of the line is pure popular song,” offering an opinion thoroughly characteristic of him. The other three therefore entrusted the entire right of translation to Yojirō.
